subject: Suitability of data set for open capture-recapture analysis, with focus on apparent survival

messages.author: 155a1734fbb87411
messages.subject: Suitability of data set for open capture-recapture analysis, with focus on apparent survival
parts:
Hello all,

My apologies if this is off-topic, in which case please ignore.

Mark-recapture is not an analytical strength of mine, so I would appreciate thoughts on the viability of an analysis of some bird color-band resighting data, primarily to estimate apparent annual survivorship estimates by age at initial capture/marking.

The data comes from Red-cockaded Woodpeckers, which arrange themselves in "breeding clusters" on the landscape made primarily of M/F breeders and zero to several helpers.

Each spring, biologists color-band the young of a cluster while in the nest. Most clusters (n = ~ 30) on the study area are visited annually, so most birds in the population are uniquely marked.

During spring banding visits and subsequent nest checks, attempts are made to identify the adult birds present in a given cluster (i.e., parents and helpers).

These birds are home-bodies. Adults rarely move between clusters. Birds banded as nestlings will show up in other clusters in subsequent years, particularly females, but rarely if ever leave the study area altogether.

In a given year, resighting effort by staff is extremely variable among clusters. Resighting effort also varies from year to year. Resighting effort is completely undocumented. Nor is any record kept of encounters with unmarked or unidentified individuals.

Most initial marking and resighting effort occurs over a short 1-2 month interval (May - June) but there are sporadic observations of birds in fall/winter. The attached image summarizes the encounter histories.

I'm a bit at a loss for what, if any, analytical framework will help us make some estimates of apparent survivorship for birds in their first year of life and subsequent years.

Any thoughts are greatly appreciated.

Best,
Adam

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: Suitability of data set for open capture-recapture analysis, with focus on apparent survival
parts:
Dear Adam,

from what I understand, you seem to have a classical, if a little dirty perhaps, data set for use in a Cormack-Jolly-Seber (CJS) model. In this model, you condition on first capture (i.e., the moment when a bird is marked) and then describe probabilistically the detection-nondetection events in later years as a function of two parameters: apparent survival and recapture probability. Apparent survival is the product of true survival and fidelity, which is the probability to remain in the study area. If you think your birds rarely leave the study area, then what the CJS gets you will be close to true survival. I say "a little dirty", because from your description, you appear to have a bit of heterogeneity (in time, between individuals, not sure...) in recapure probability. Very old, classical, conventional wisdom (I think, something like Carothers 1973) says that CJS survival estimates are pretty robust to heterogeneity in recapture (unlike for instance N estimates in closed-population models), although this may be a little too optimistic, i.e., I think a paper where David Fletcher was one of the authors found otherwise. But notwithstanding, I think I would put your data set into a CJS model. Run GoF tests through program RELEASE (from MARK) and you can fit the model in MARK or else in BUGS, too: easiest to use code from the BPA book in the latter case. Due to the grouping of individuals in clusters, you might want to fit the model in BUGS and have a random clister effect to account for the possible non-independence of fates of individuals in the same cluster.

Just some ideas, best regards  --- Marc
